paras: The lynching of Tom Stewart was the hanging of a man accused of double murder by masked men who took him from his captor near Old Agency, on the Teton in Montana Territory, on the evening of July 1, 1881. Stewart, whom the Fort Benton River Press named Brackett E. Stewart, was accused of killing O. H. Morgan and Mrs. Annie Armstrong and burning their house two days earlier. A coroner's jury found him hanged by persons unknown, and the Montana papers presented the lynching as deserved punishment.

According to a Fort Shaw dispatch to the Helena Herald, Morgan and Mrs. Armstrong were murdered in their house near the mouth of the Muddy, on the Teton, early on June 29, and the house and bodies were burned. Two girls living with Mrs. Armstrong escaped, and the elder said a man had killed the two adults, searched the trunks for money and set the fire. The Herald added that Mrs. Armstrong, a former Helena resident, was of French and Indian descent.

Maggie Housman, twelve, testified that the killer shot Morgan upstairs, then shot Mrs. Armstrong and went through the trunks, and six-year-old Annie Keogh corroborated her. The girls fled on a mare and met H. L. Kennerly on the road.

Kennerly recognized Stewart from their description, and he and A. B. Hamilton arrested him after Maggie picked him out of about fifteen men in front of the store. Stewart was found with a pair of blankets said to be Mrs. Armstrong's and, according to the Herald's correspondent, one hundred dollars that her son said was all the money in the house. The same correspondent wrote that when the girls pointed him out, Stewart said he had nothing more to say.

On Friday evening, July 1, a party of masked men rode up to Hamilton as he was taking Stewart to Benton, leveled their guns at him and demanded the prisoner. By the River Press account, about twenty more men then joined them, took Stewart by force and hanged him from a tree near Hamilton & Hazlett's place at Old Agency. Stewart showed no emotion and asked only that they break his neck; the Herald reported him found hanging with his neck broken. A visitor to Old Agency later told the River Press that each of the lynchers took a piece of the rope as a relic and that Stewart's belongings were divided among "the committee."

A coroner's inquest was held over the body before Judge Tattan, where Hamilton swore that he did not recognize any of the party and could not identify them. The jury's verdict was that Stewart "came to his death by hanging" and that the hanging was committed "by persons to the jury unknown." Stewart was buried in a shallow grave near the spot. No report of arrests of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and by mid-July the Benton Weekly Record reported the excitement on the Teton had subsided.

Weeklies in Fort Benton, Helena and Butte covered the case, and none gave Stewart's race. The Helena Herald's Fort Shaw dispatch announced that the man who murdered Mrs. Armstrong and Morgan "is no more" and declared his guilt positively established, and the Butte Weekly Miner reprinted it under the headline "LYNCHED. Tom Stewart Swings for a Double Murder." The River Press headed its account "Lynching of the Teton Murderer," called Stewart a "fiend in human shape," and wrote that although lynch law was "to be deprecated," the community would "hardly find fault with the swift retribution."

The Benton Weekly Record listed Stewart's hanging alongside the lynching of a man named Jones in the Judith Basin and other recent incidents as "a warning to malefactors in our midst." The Bismarck Tribune, quoting the Yellowstone Journal, placed the cabin on the Missouri and added only that the murderer had been lynched.

The papers differed on the accused man's first name: the River Press called him Brackett E. Stewart, while the Herald dispatch and the Weekly Miner called him Tom Stewart. The River Press, drawing on Hamilton's sworn testimony, put the party at a masked group joined by about twenty more; the Herald's correspondent said fifteen men.

reader.title: Lynching of Tom Stewart
bases: Masked armed men took the accused man from A. B. Hamilton and hanged him from a tree, and a coroner's jury found he was hanged by persons unknown (A2, A3, A4).

Stewart was hanged by a party of fifteen to twenty or more masked men who seized him from the man taking him to Benton, without legal authority (the papers call it 'lynch law' and the coroner's jury found 'persons unknown'), as punishment for the murders of Morgan and Mrs. Armstrong (A2, A3, A4, A7).

The Fort Benton River Press, drawing on sworn inquest testimony, and the Helena Herald's separate Fort Shaw correspondent agree that the accused was taken from Hamilton by a party of men and hanged (A2, A3, A4); the Benton Weekly Record and Bismarck Tribune also report the hanging (A10, A11).

The Helena Herald's dispatch declared Stewart's guilt 'positively established' beyond 'a shadow of doubt'; the Butte Weekly Miner reprinted it as 'LYNCHED. Tom Stewart Swings for a Double Murder.'

The Bismarck Tribune, quoting the Yellowstone Journal, described the murders and noted only that the murderer had been lynched.
